title: Open my lips (Psalm 51:17)
hook: "O Lord, open Thou my lips", the Amidah's first line

segments.voice: Yesterday, the doorway into the Amidah. Your line was three steps in. Did you take them before something that mattered? Now you're standing in place. Today, the very first words. Day five hundred seventy-five.

Everyone knows the moment. You've rehearsed it in the car. You walk into the room, the person looks up, and nothing comes out. Or the wrong thing comes out. A job interview, a hospital bed, an apology you've owed for a year. The words were there an hour ago. The Amidah is the most important speech of the Jewish day, and it starts by admitting exactly this. Before a single blessing, the person praying asks for help just to speak.
screen: `YOU REHEARSED IT IN THE CAR.` → `NOTHING COMES OUT.` → `THE PRAYER STARTS BY ADMITTING IT.`

segments.voice: The line comes from Psalm 51, a psalm of a broken person asking to be made whole again. In the old Jewish translation: "O Lord, open Thou my lips; and my mouth shall declare Thy praise." In Hebrew, Adonai sefatai tiftach. Notice the order. Not: I will praise You. But: You open, and then my mouth will praise. Even the ability to pray is asked for, not assumed. The rabbis placed this verse right at the threshold of the Amidah, said quietly after the three steps. But it raised a problem. We learned two days ago: no gap between redemption and the Amidah. So isn't this verse an interruption? The Talmud, in Berakhot, answers: no. Since the rabbis established it as part of the prayer, it counts as one long Amidah. The verse isn't a pause before the prayer. It's the prayer's front door, already inside. There's a lovely honesty here. The Amidah will go on to praise God as great and mighty, ask for wisdom, for healing, for peace. Big words. And it begins by saying: left to myself, I might not get them out. It's a speaker tapping the microphone, and finding out the power comes from somewhere else. And it can be said by anyone, before anything: before a hard conversation, before teaching a class, before a toast. Open my lips. Let what comes out be worth hearing.
screen: `FROM PSALM 51.` · `YOU OPEN, THEN I PRAISE.` · `NOT A GAP: THE FRONT DOOR.` · `EVEN SPEAKING IS ASKED FOR.` · then, large: `OPEN MY LIPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask to speak well today. Settle, and breathe. Think of the most important thing you'll say today. Maybe it's a hard conversation, maybe just a kind word you keep meaning to say. Picture the moment just before. Now, if you pray, you can say the psalm's line, quietly: O Lord, open Thou my lips. If you don't, hold the wish in your own way: that the right words come, and the wrong ones don't. Breathe in on the wish. Breathe out ready. The bell holds the time.
Open my lips. Adonai sefatai tiftach. The verse from Psalm 51 that opens the Amidah, asking for help to speak before speaking.
Your line: open my lips. Today, before your hardest conversation, take one breath and ask, in whatever way is yours, for the right words. Day five hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Jews say Adonai sefatai tiftach, "O Lord, open my lips", quietly at the start of every Amidah, right after taking the three steps forward; it's treated as part of the Amidah itself.
